main.title: Summer Carnival '92: Recca
main.subtitle: Recca Pushes the Famicom Until It Looks Like a Faster Machine
main.summary: On July 17, 1992 Naxat Soft released Summer Carnival '92: Recca for Famicom in Japan.

cards.heading: Pushing the Famicom to its limits
cards.text: Naxat Soft released KID's Summer Carnival '92: Recca for the Famicom in Japan on July 17, 1992. Designed around the Summer Carnival tournament tradition, the vertical shooter combines fast enemy formations, several weapon types and timed challenges. Nintendo later highlighted its unusually rapid action on NES hardware. Scoring modes provide short sections to practise and compare.

cards.heading: Weapons and satellites
cards.text: The Recca ship can carry five different main weapons, each with advantages and disadvantages. Weapon icons dropped by enemies equip or upgrade them. Five kinds of sub-weapon supply satellite-like options that shoot in different directions. Clearing normal mode unlocks a harder second loop with seven rearranged stages.

cards.heading: A shield built by holding fire
cards.text: When the player stops firing the main weapon briefly, an energy shield charges in front of the ship. It absorbs ordinary enemy projectiles and can be launched to destroy enemies within its blast radius. Firing continuously and preparing this defence therefore require different timings.

cards.heading: Racing the clock
cards.text: Score Attack asks the player to earn as many points as possible in two minutes. Time Attack instead measures how quickly two stages can be completed within five minutes. A hidden Zanki Attack mode starts with fifty lives, but defeated enemies release suicide bullets; remaining lives contribute to the final bonus.

main.title: Thunder Force IV
main.subtitle: Thunder Force IV Uses Scrolling as Spectacle and Information
main.summary: On July 24, 1992 Technosoft released Thunder Force IV for Mega Drive in Japan.

cards.heading: A battlefield beyond the screen
cards.text: On July 24, 1992 Technosoft released Thunder Force IV for Mega Drive in Japan. The horizontal shooter expands the series' scale with stages taller than the screen, multiple scrolling layers and an arsenal that can be switched during play. The player must read ship position, terrain and available weapons at the same time while the soundtrack pushes the hardware toward an aggressive sonic identity. Its reputation comes from the meeting of technique and control: the console appears to show more than the screen can contain, yet the action remains readable.

cards.heading: A battlefield larger than the screen
cards.text: Thunder Force IV is a horizontal shoot 'em up. The story takes place two years after the events of Thunder Force III. The player takes on the role of a fighter pilot to battle the Orn Empire, which is plotting the extinction of the human race. The first four stages can be selected in any order. There are ten stages total. They scroll horizontally automatically, and the player can also explore up and down to scroll the screen vertically and reveal a larger playing field. The player can change the speed of their ship at any time for easier maneuverability. Scrolling up and down will reveal different waves of enemies the player can shoot down, as well as hidden power-ups. At the end of each stage is a boss, and sometimes there are bosses mid-stage.

cards.heading: An arsenal for different situations
cards.text: Some enemies will drop power-ups that if picked up by the player will arm the ship with new weaponry, including a variety of missiles and lasers that fire in different patterns. Each weapon has advantages and drawbacks, and is more or less effective depending on the battle situation the player finds themselves in. The player can hold multiple weapons and cycle through them at will. Other power-ups include shields and satellite ships that revolve around their ship and multiply their firepower. Half-way through the game, the player gains a powerful "Thunder Sword" attack which deals massive damage to enemies. It requires that the player have two satellite ships.

cards.heading: Making an FM guitar sound
cards.text: The sound team, led by Naosuke Arai, were fans of heavy metal and tried to create the sound of an electric guitar using the Mega Drive's FM synthesizer. After encountering difficulties, they used the system's distortion sound effects to achieve the result. The rest of the development team had previously worked on the Mega Drive conversion of Devil's Crush.

main.title: Super Mario Kart
main.subtitle: Racing Became a Language for Playing Together
main.summary: Nintendo released Super Mario Kart in Japan for the Super Famicom on August 27, 1992.

cards.heading: Racing Became a Language for Playing Together
cards.text: Nintendo released Super Mario Kart for the Super Famicom in Japan on August 27, 1992. The project began as an attempt to make an F-Zero-like race for two players. Compact tracks and slower karts suited the split-screen display; Mario's characters, shells and bananas were added later. Driving skill and direct interference with opponents became parts of the same race.

cards.heading: The Project Begins with the Problem of Letting Two People Race Together
cards.text: Hideki Konno recalled Miyamoto asking for a two-player game resembling F-Zero. Its long straights and high speed proved impractical in split screen. The team reduced the pace and built smaller courses around vehicles readable in the available space. These decisions established the racing format before Mario and the items joined it.

cards.heading: Rotating the Plane Creates the Feeling of Racing Inside the Map
cards.text: Mode 7 rotates and scales a flat graphical plane to present the course in perspective. Kart sprites and the camera complete the effect. The circuits need to remain compact and recognisable in each half of the screen, with curves and obstacles players can anticipate while moving. Their arrangement is closely connected to how the hardware displays the track.

cards.heading: The Shell Turns Racing into an Aggressive Conversation
cards.text: Shells, banana peels and other items allow racers to affect one another directly. Keeping an item for protection, throwing it immediately or waiting for a better position adds a choice alongside steering. A good racing line can gain time, but an opponent still has opportunities to interfere. Players must judge both the track and the distance to other karts.

main.title: Dragon Quest V
main.summary: Dragon Quest V: Hand of the Heavenly Bride, known in Europe as Dragon Quest: The Hand of the Heavenly Bride and in Japan as Dragon Quest V: Bride of Heaven, is a 1992 role-playing video game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix for the Super Famicom.

cards.text: Dragon Quest V: Hand of the Heavenly Bride, known in Europe as Dragon Quest: The Hand of the Heavenly Bride and in Japan as Dragon Quest V: Bride of Heaven, is a 1992 role-playing video game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix for the Super Famicom. The fifth main installment in the Dragon Quest series, the game was the first title in the franchise to not be initially localized in North America due to programming issues.

It later had an enhanced remake only in Japan for the PlayStation 2 in 2004. The remake was developed by ArtePiazza and Matrix Software. Another remake was made for the Nintendo DS, which was released in Japan in July 2008 and worldwide in February 2009; this marks the first time the game had officially released in English. In addition, ports for Android and iOS were released in Japan in December 2014, and worldwide the following month.

The story spans roughly thirty years, following the protagonist from childhood through marriage and raising a family. Monsters met in random encounters can offer to join the party, a system later used in other Dragon Quest games and made central to Dragon Quest Monsters. Megami Tensei had already explored recruiting monsters, while Pokémon, Digimon and other series later developed their own collection systems. The protagonist's family life, including a playable period during pregnancy, also became a distinctive part of the game's reputation. The animated adaptation Dragon Quest: Your Story was released in Japan in 2019 and later internationally through Netflix.

main.title: Air Zonk
main.subtitle: Bonk’s future takes flight
main.summary: Air Zonk is Red Company's cartoon shooter, released for TurboGrafx-16 in North America in October 1992.

cards.heading: Bonk’s future takes flight
cards.text: Air Zonk is Red Company's cartoon shooter, released for TurboGrafx-16 in North America in October 1992. Zonk resembles Bonk, but sunglasses and cybernetic powers place this hero in a comic future. He flies through five scrolling stages against King Drool's machines, choosing a companion before the action begins. The resemblance connects the game to an established mascot while the constant flight supplies a different kind of adventure, built around shooting, charged attacks and the surprising shapes taken by Zonk's friends.

cards.heading: A companion becomes a new weapon
cards.text: Collecting eight smiley faces summons the selected friend, who follows Zonk and adds supporting fire. Another set lets the pair merge into a hybrid with a new attack and a period of invulnerability. Each companion is available once, so choosing when to use a particular friend shapes the journey through the stages. The combinations make the cast part of the weapon system. A strange character encountered in the selection screen becomes a practical advantage whose movement and attack can change the next stretch of play.

cards.heading: A mascot with a different attitude
cards.text: Holding a shot charges an attack, while a longer charge produces a screen-wide bomb. Seven weapon power-ups provide further variations, each with a special charged form. Difficulty choices and friend settings let players adjust the challenge. Red Company developed the game with Naxat Soft, and Daisuke Morishima and Hisashi Matsushita composed its music. Air Zonk turns the familiar prehistoric world into a playful technological one, retaining its expressive creatures while making unlikely partnerships and transformations the center of the shooting.

main.title: Mortal Kombat
main.subtitle: Fighting Finds Another Face
main.summary: On October 8, 1992, Mortal Kombat debuted in U.S. arcades.

cards.heading: Fighting Finds Another Face
cards.text: Midway's Mortal Kombat debuted in American arcades on October 8, 1992. Ed Boon, John Tobias and a small team built its fighters from digitised performers, combining recognisable bodies with supernatural moves. A dedicated block button and Fatality finishers distinguished its matches. The later home releases also became prominent in public debate about game violence.

cards.heading: Real People Inside an Impossible Fiction
cards.text: The team filmed real performers' poses and movements, then selected and adapted the images into sprites. Tobias connected the game's rougher appearance to this digitisation process. Recorded bodies could perform exaggerated attacks against fantastical opponents and backgrounds. Their movements still needed to communicate a useful attack or defensive action during a fight.

cards.heading: Five buttons, shared attacks and blocking
cards.text: Mortal Kombat uses an 8-directional joystick and 5 buttons, including 2 punch and 2 kick buttons, each further differentiated between high and low. Attacks can vary depending on the player's distance from the opponent. All player characters have a shared set of attacks performed by holding the joystick in various directions, such as a leg sweep and an uppercut. The latter attack knocks the enemy high into the air and causes much damage. Most special moves were performed by tapping the joystick, sometimes ending with a button press. Unlike previous one-on-one fighting games, few moves require circular joystick movement. The game's blocking system also distinguished itself from other fighting games, as characters take a small amount of damage from regular moves while blocking. However, the dedicated block button allows users to defend against attacks without retreating. Blocking characters lose very little ground when struck, thus making counterattacks much easier after a successful block.

cards.heading: Shang Tsung, Goro and the tournament
cards.text: The game takes place in Earthrealm, where a tournament is being held on Shang Tsung's Island, on which seven of its locations serve as stages in the game. The introduction to Mortal Kombat explains that Shang Tsung was banished to Earthrealm 500 years ago and, with the help of the monstrous Goro, seized control of the Mortal Kombat tournament in an attempt to doom the realm. For 500 years straight, Goro has been undefeated in the tournament and has won nine consecutive tournaments. If Goro wins again, Shao Kahn, Emperor of Outworld, will be allowed to take Earthrealm. To prevent this, a new generation of warriors must challenge Goro.

cards.heading: Juggling and Fatalities
cards.text: Mortal Kombat further introduced the concept of "juggling", knocking an opponent into the air and following up with a combination of attacks while the enemy is still airborne and defenseless. The idea became so popular that it spread to many other games. Another of the game's innovations was the Fatality, a finishing move performed against a defeated opponent to execute them in a gruesome fashion.

cards.heading: Goro Is Born as a Special Effect
cards.text: Goro required a different method from the human fighters. The team built an articulated puppet and digitised its poses, turning a physical special effect into arcade sprites. His size and four arms made the tournament's boss immediately distinct from the filmed performers. The two production techniques appeared together within the same setting.

cards.heading: Violence Leaves the Arcade
cards.text: Mortal Kombat reached home consoles in 1993 and was cited in United States Senate hearings about violent games. The controversy helped create the conditions for the industry's ESRB ratings system in 1994. A game designed to attract attention in an arcade was now being discussed in relation to household audiences, advertising and information for parents.

features.title: Who gets to rate a game?
features.summary: From a hearing to a label.

cards.heading: The question put to the industry
cards.text: Senators Joseph Lieberman and Herb Kohl held a joint hearing on violent games and information for parents on December 9, 1993. Educators and industry representatives testified, including Nintendo's Howard Lincoln and Sega's Bill White. The committee's report records a commitment from industry representatives to create a ratings system for the 1994 holiday season.

cards.heading: Independence becomes a requirement
cards.text: A second hearing on March 4, 1994 examined the industry's preliminary proposal. Independence and credibility were central questions, and retail representatives supported participating. A working scheme needed publishers and shops to recognise the same process, giving its labels practical value wherever a game was sold.

cards.heading: An industry body makes categories
cards.text: The ESRB was established in 1994 under the Interactive Digital Software Association. Its initial announcement set out five rating categories and seventeen content descriptors. Age recommendations and descriptions of material inside the game supplied different kinds of information, allowing a label to identify more than a single recommended audience.

cards.heading: The label keeps changing
cards.text: The system continued to develop after its introduction. An advertising code followed in 1995, Kids to Adults became Everyone in 1998, and an Advertising Review Council was created in 2000. That year also brought a sanctions system with points, fines and corrective action. Content ratings and oversight of how companies promoted their games became related responsibilities.

main.title: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins
main.summary: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins is a 1992 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy.

cards.heading: Reclaiming Mario Land from Wario
cards.text: Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins is a 1992 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy. It is the sequel to Super Mario Land. In Super Mario Land 2, the player assumes the role of the protagonist Mario, whose main objective is to reclaim his personal island, Mario Land, from the clutches of his greedy rival Wario. The gameplay builds and expands on that of its precursor with innovations carried over from Super Mario World and Super Mario Bros. 3.

cards.heading: Wario debuts and the game returns
cards.text: Super Mario Land 2 received critical acclaim upon release and sold over 11 million copies, becoming one of the most successful and highest-rated titles on the Game Boy. Reviewers emphasized that the game surpassed its predecessor in all aspects. Super Mario Land 2 marks the debut appearance of Wario, who would become a prominent character in the Super Mario series as the antihero of several games, the first being this game's sequel Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3. Super Mario Land 2 was re-released in 2011 as a downloadable title for the Nintendo 3DS, and the Nintendo Switch in 2023, as part of the Nintendo Classics service.

main.title: Landstalker
main.subtitle: A treasure hunt with depth
main.summary: Nigel’s search for King Nole’s treasure turns isometric rooms into puzzles of height, movement and perspective.

cards.heading: Nigel and the treasure
cards.text: Landstalker is Climax Entertainment’s action adventure for Mega Drive, first released in Japan on 30 October 1992. Nigel, a treasure hunter, travels with the fairy Friday in search of the riches of King Nole. Towns, outdoor paths and dungeons all use an isometric view, giving the journey a consistent sense of height and depth. Sword fighting shares the same space with jumping, conversations and movable objects. Progress comes from understanding how those everyday actions fit the room in front of Nigel, as well as defeating its monsters.

cards.heading: Finding the height of a jump
cards.text: A platform may appear close to another while sitting at a different height, so judging a jump becomes a small spatial puzzle. Blocks can provide steps, switches can open a route, and a locked door may require a detour before Nigel returns with its key. The same diagonal view also frames combat, making position important when approaching an enemy with the sword. Rather than separating puzzles into a different screen, the game places monsters, traps and routes together inside spaces the player has to read carefully.

cards.heading: Tools for the next room
cards.text: Nigel starts with a compact set of actions: walking, jumping, swinging his sword, climbing and lifting objects. New equipment improves his strength and protection, while items help him survive or open the next part of the adventure. Because those basic movements remain familiar, later rooms can ask more demanding questions of the same skills. The journey also returns to earlier towns and dungeons, turning remembered places into useful landmarks. Motoaki Takenouchi’s score accompanies this treasure hunt through a world built from interlocking rooms and paths.

main.title: Landstalker: The Treasures of King Nole
main.subtitle: An island measured in jumps
main.summary: Landstalker arrived on the Japanese Mega Drive on October 30, 1992. Climax’s adventure pairs a treasure hunter with the small, flying Friday in a search for a legendary fortune. Its distinctive isometric view makes towns, caves and ruins look like connected miniature spaces. That angle is more than a visual signature: platforms can overlap, paths can hide behind walls, and the player must judge height as well as direction. Reaching the next ledge can demand as much attention as winning a sword fight.

cards.heading: Treasure viewed from an angle
cards.text: Landstalker arrived on the Japanese Mega Drive on October 30, 1992. Climax’s adventure pairs a treasure hunter with the small, flying Friday in a search for a legendary fortune. Its distinctive isometric view makes towns, caves and ruins look like connected miniature spaces. That angle is more than a visual signature: platforms can overlap, paths can hide behind walls, and the player must judge height as well as direction. cards.heading: Reading the height of a room
cards.text: Fields, dungeons and event scenes share an isometric view, with jumping, attacks and movable objects used throughout. Blocks, switches and moving platforms make rooms problems of position and timing. Conversations in the island's settlements connect these challenges to the wider journey, with Friday accompanying the treasure hunter. Motoaki Takenouchi composed the original Mega Drive score.

main.title: Shin Megami Tensei
main.summary: Shin Megami Tensei is a role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the Super Famicom.

cards.heading: Demons become allies
cards.text: Shin Megami Tensei is a role-playing video game developed and published by Atlus for the Super Famicom. Originally released in 1992 in Japan, it has been ported to multiple systems and eventually released in the West for iOS in 2014. It was released on the Virtual Console service in Japan on Wii in 2007 and on Wii U in 2013, as well as the Nintendo Classics service in 2020. It is the third game in the Megami Tensei series and the first in the central Shin Megami Tensei series. The gameplay uses first-person navigation of dungeons and turn-based battles against demons. The player can recruit demons as allies by talking to them rather than fighting them, and two to three demons can be fused to create new demons.

cards.heading: Tokyo between law and chaos
cards.text: The story follows a player-named protagonist who lives in near-future Tokyo. When a portal to the realm of demons is opened accidentally by a scientist named Steven and is seized by Gotou, a military commander who believes that he can control the demons, the United States government orders a nuclear attack on Tokyo. Transported with two other supporting characters thirty years into the future, the protagonist finds the Earth ruined by a demon invasion, which is now the stage for an escalating conflict between the Order of Messiah and the Ring of Gaia, conflicting cults who wish to bring about kingdoms for their respective patron deities (Yahweh and Lucifer). The story is influenced by moral decisions the protagonist makes, aligning him either with the Messians, the Ring of Gaia, or setting him up as an independent agent.

cards.heading: An identity for Atlus
cards.text: From the start of the production, Atlus staff saw Shin Megami Tensei as a chance to create a game with the company's brand on it. The staff saw it as a remake of the previous Megami Tensei game; because of this, they knew what was going to happen in the story, and the development went smoothly. The story went through multiple revisions, and many settings were inspired by the staff's personal lives. The character and demon designs were done by Kazuma Kaneko, who used mythical figures and multiple clothing styles in his designs. Critical and commercial reception for the game have been highly positive, and its success helped launch Atlus as a developer and publisher, along with popularizing the Megami Tensei series.
